newsitem.title: USA: Republic of Texas security chief surrenders.
newsitem.headline: Republic of Texas security chief surrenders.

text.p: A key member of the armed Republic of Texas separatists holed up in the west Texas mountains surrendered on Friday as police continued to seek a peaceful end to the six-day standoff.

Police said the surrender of Robert Scheidt, the group's chief of security, was a hopeful sign they could negotiate an end to the standoff with a dozen armed militia still defending the group's dusty "embassy" in the Davis Mountains.
"We are encouraged that none of our contingency planning is going to have to come into effect, at least in the immediate term," Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox said.

Scheidt is one of six Republic of Texas members including the group's leader, Richard McLaren, who face state felony charges for engaging in criminal activity. Three of the six also are charged with aggravated kidnapping.
The standoff was sparked by Scheidt's arrest on Sunday on arms charges. He was returned to the compound hours later in return for release of two neighbours taken hostage by the group in retaliation.

"He walked out of the compound and was arrested by two DPS troopers without incident," Cox said of Scheidt's surrender on Friday. Scheidt was taken into custody and would be jailed in the nearby town of Marfa later on Friday, he said.

McLaren, 43, still has not responded to what his attorney, Terence O'Rourke termed as an ultimatum from police on Thursday calling for his surrender. Scheidt carried out a package of documents from McLaren to be delivered to O'Rourke, Cox said.

Police have surrounded the complex and brought in helicopters, two police armoured personnel carriers and bloodhounds. They have pledged to execute the arrest warrants if they cannot negotiate a peaceful end to the standoff.

Officials said they were concerned the siege was becoming a rallying point for anti-government militias after arresting at least nine armed men in the area this week on their way to fight alongside the separatists.

The Republic of Texas group, formed in 1995, believes the 1845 annexation of Texas by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836.
McLaren resumed communications with police on Thursday after two days of silence from his ramshackle hideout where the group has mounted its campaign for Texas' independence.

Before he broke off talks, police had indicated his surrender was near and the siege would end quickly and peacefully. But on Thursday, they cut off electricity to the compound and said they had made their final offer.
"It is now in his court to respond to this," said Cox, who declined to give details of the offer and did not say how long McLaren had to respond.
Cox stressed that officials still wanted a peaceful solution to the crisis.
"We have said all along we want a peaceful outcome to this, not a Wild West outcome," said Cox.
